title: Clear pronoun reference
blurb: Spot pronouns that point two ways, point nowhere or point to a whole idea, and rewrite them so only one reading is possible.
question: A shift note reads, “When the nurse called the patient's daughter, she was upset, and this delayed the discharge. They say it happens often.” Which pronouns are unclear, and how would you fix them?

teach.h: Every pronoun needs one clear antecedent
teach.body: Formally, a pronoun's antecedent is the noun it stands for, and clear reference means the reader can identify exactly one antecedent for every pronoun. Plain English: when you read “she,” “it,” “they” or “this,” you should be able to point at one word earlier in the sentence and say “that one.” If you can point at two words, or at none, the reference is unclear and the HESI A2 counts it as an error to fix.

teach.h: Three ways a reference goes wrong

children.label: Ambiguous
children.sub: When Maya called Rosa, she cried.

children.label: Vague
children.sub: In the article, they say rest helps.

children.label: Broad
children.sub: He was late and lost his badge, and this ...

teach.caption: Fix all three by naming the noun, or by rebuilding the sentence so only one noun fits.

rows.label: Two people
values: Tom told Jaden his badge expired.

rows.label: Two things
values: She set the vial on the tray, and it cracked.
The vial cracked when she set it on the tray.

rows.label: Two groups
values: The nurses told the patients they would move.
The nurses said the patients would move.

teach.caption: Adding a word (“own,” “now,” “suddenly”) never fixes ambiguity: the pronoun still has two possible antecedents.

head: Vague
Problem
Fix
rows: At the clinic, they told me ...
Ty wants to be a nurse; it pays well.

teach.body: “This,” “that” and “which” sometimes point back to a whole idea instead of a noun. That is clear only when one idea is possible. “The aide arrived late and skipped the safety briefing, and this worried the charge nurse”: was it the lateness, the skipped briefing or both? Name the idea: “The aide's skipped safety briefing worried the charge nurse.” Adding a noun after this (“this delay”) also works.

rows.label: a student → you
values: If a student studies, you pass.

rows.label: students → we
values: If students rest, we feel better.
If students rest, they feel better.

teach.caption: Person: first (I, we), second (you), third (he, she, it, one, they, any noun). Keep one person for the same people.

teach.h: Scenario: Leah rewrites a shift note
teach.body: Nursing applicant Leah Brooks, a unit clerk, revises: “When the nurse called the patient's daughter, she was upset, and this delayed the discharge. They say it happens often.” “She” could be the nurse or the daughter, so Leah writes “the daughter was upset.” “This” could mean the call or the upset, so she writes “her concerns delayed the discharge.” “They” names no one, so she writes “The unit manager says such delays happen often.”

teach.text: The HESI A2 offers “fixes” that only decorate the sentence: adding “own,” “carefully” or “then,” moving a phrase, or switching to the passive voice. If the pronoun can still point to two nouns, or to none, the sentence is still unclear. Only naming the noun or rebuilding the sentence fixes it.

items: Point test: you must be able to point to exactly one antecedent for every pronoun.
Ambiguous = two possible antecedents; vague = none; broad = a whole idea that could be more than one thing.
Fix by naming the noun, using a direct quotation, or rebuilding the sentence.
Decorating words (own, now, carefully) and passive voice do not fix ambiguity.
Keep the same person: no shift from one or a student to you or we.

summary: You can now spot ambiguous, vague and broad pronouns and pick the revision that leaves only one possible antecedent. You can also catch shifts in person, such as one or a student followed by you.

A.q: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?
options: After Rosa met Maya at the library, she felt calmer.
Rosa was upset about the exam when she called Maya.
On the news, they said the clinic will expand soon.
Tom told Jaden that his badge had expired today.
A.why: “She” is the subject of “called,” and the person called is Maya, so “she” can only be Rosa.

whyNot.0: “She” could be Rosa or Maya, so the reference is ambiguous.
whyNot.2: “They” has no antecedent; name the source (the reporter, the hospital).
whyNot.3: “His” could mean Tom's badge or Jaden's badge, so the reference is ambiguous.

A.q: Which revision fixes the unclear pronoun in “After the nurse spoke with the patient, she went home”?
options: After speaking with the patient, the nurse went home.
After the nurse spoke with the patient, they went home.
After the nurse spoke with the patient, she then went home.
After the nurse spoke with the patient, her shift ended.
A.why: Naming the nurse as the subject removes any doubt about who went home.

whyNot.1: “They” is still unclear: it could mean the nurse, the patient or both.
whyNot.2: Adding “then” does nothing to show whether “she” is the nurse or the patient.
whyNot.3: “Her” could still be the nurse or the patient, so the reference stays ambiguous.

A.q: Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun?
options: In the handout, it explains how to use the inhaler.
They recommend using the inhaler before exercise.
The handout explains how to use the inhaler.
At the pharmacy, they showed how to use it properly.
A.why: The handout is named as the subject, so no pronoun is left without an antecedent.

whyNot.0: “It” has no noun to refer to; the handout itself should be the subject.
whyNot.1: “They” names no one; say who recommends it.
whyNot.3: “They” names no people, and “it” has no antecedent.

B.q: Which revision corrects the shift in person in “When a nurse starts a new job, you often feel overwhelmed”?
options: When a nurse starts a new job, we often feel overwhelmed.
When nurses start a new job, they often feel overwhelmed.
When a nurse starts a new job, I often feel overwhelmed.
When nurses start a new job, you often feel overwhelmed.
B.why: “Nurses” and “they” are both third person plural, so person and number match.

whyNot.0: Shifts from third person (a nurse) to first person (we).
whyNot.2: Shifts from third person (a nurse) to first person (I).
whyNot.3: Shifts from third person (nurses) to second person (you).

B.q: Which revision of “Kevin told Malik that he had passed the HESI A2” makes the pronoun reference clear?
options: Kevin told Malik that he had finally passed the HESI A2.
Kevin told Malik, “I passed the HESI A2.”
Kevin told Malik that he himself had passed the HESI A2.
Kevin and Malik were told that he passed the HESI A2.
B.why: In the direct quotation, “I” can only be Kevin, the speaker.

whyNot.0: Adding “finally” leaves “he” pointing to either Kevin or Malik.
whyNot.2: “He himself” could still be either man.
whyNot.3: “He” now has two possible antecedents in the subject.

B.q: Which revision makes the broad “this” clear in “Ana skipped lunch and forgot her water bottle, and this gave her a headache”?
options: Ana skipped lunch and forgot her water bottle, and this then gave her a headache.
Ana skipped lunch and forgot her water bottle; this gave her a headache.
Ana skipped lunch and forgot her water bottle, and it gave her a headache.
Skipping lunch and going without water gave Ana a headache.
B.why: Naming both causes as the subject removes the pronoun, so there is no doubt about what gave her the headache.

whyNot.0: Adding “then” leaves “this” pointing to either action or both.
whyNot.1: Changing the punctuation does not tell the reader what “this” means.
whyNot.2: “It” is just as unclear: it could even point to the water bottle.

C.q: Which sentence contains an ambiguous pronoun?
options: Before Luis met Dev at the gym, he had not lifted weights.
Luis had not lifted weights before he met Dev at the gym.
The nurse checked the monitor because its alarm was beeping.
Dr. Ames said she would call the patient after lunch.
C.why: “He” comes after both names in the opening clause, so it could mean Luis or Dev.

whyNot.1: “He” met Dev, so “he” must be Luis; nobody meets himself.
whyNot.2: “Its” can only mean the monitor, the thing with an alarm.
whyNot.3: “She” is the one who will call the patient, so it points to Dr. Ames.

C.q: Which revision of “The doctors told the interns that they would present at grand rounds” makes the reference clear?
options: The doctors told the interns that they would all present at grand rounds.
The interns were told by the doctors that they would present at grand rounds.
The doctors told the interns, “You will present at grand rounds.”
The doctors told the interns that they would present at their grand rounds.
C.why: In the quotation, “you” can only mean the interns, the people being spoken to.

whyNot.0: Adding “all” leaves “they” pointing to the doctors or the interns.
whyNot.1: The passive voice keeps “they” with two possible antecedents.
whyNot.3: “They” and “their” could each mean either group.

C.q: Which sentence keeps the same pronoun person throughout?
options: If one forgets to log out, you may lose your work.
If you forget to log out, you may lose your work.
If a user forgets to log out, you may lose the work.
If you forget to log out, one may lose one's work.
C.why: “You ... you ... your” stays in the second person throughout.

whyNot.0: Shifts from third person (one) to second person (you, your).
whyNot.2: Shifts from third person (a user) to second person (you).
whyNot.3: Shifts from second person (you) to third person (one, one's).

reteach.title: A pronoun is a pointing finger
reteach.question: Picture every pronoun as a finger pointing back at a person or thing already in the room. What goes wrong if two people stand together, or if the room is empty?

blocks.body: If you point at a pair of nurses and say “she,” nobody knows which one you mean: that is an ambiguous pronoun. If you point into an empty hallway and say “they,” nobody is there: that is a vague pronoun. If you wave at a whole messy room and say “this,” the listener has to guess what part you mean: that is a broad pronoun. Clear writing points at one target, every time.

blocks.text: Pointing harder does not help: adding “own,” “herself” or “now” to a pronoun with two targets leaves both targets standing.

explain.body: A pronoun is ambiguous when two nouns before it could both be its antecedent. Replace the pronoun with the noun, use a direct quotation, or rebuild the sentence so only one noun fits.

steps.label: List the nouns it could mean

test.q: Which revision of “When Ella handed Dana the form, she smiled” removes the ambiguity?
options: When Ella handed Dana the form, she smiled warmly.
Dana smiled when Ella handed her the form.
When Ella handed Dana the form, they smiled.
Ella handed Dana the form, and she smiled.
test.why: Dana is named as the one who smiled, and “her” can only mean Dana, the person handed the form.

whyNot.0: “Warmly” does not show whether Ella or Dana smiled.
whyNot.2: “They” now suggests both women, which changes the meaning and is still unclear.
whyNot.3: Joining the clauses with “and” keeps “she” pointing to either woman.

explain.body: A vague pronoun has no antecedent: “they” with no people named, “it” with no thing named. Name the real source or subject.

rows.label: they
values: The FDA says it is safe.

test.q: Which sentence contains a vague pronoun?
options: The label says to take one tablet daily.
On the label, it says to take one tablet daily.
Dr. Ames said she would refill the tablets.
The pharmacy posted its holiday hours online.
test.why: “It” has no noun to stand for; the label itself should be the subject.

whyNot.0: The label is named as the subject, so no pronoun is used.

explain.body: “This,” “that” and “which” can point to a whole idea. When the sentence holds two or more ideas, name the one you mean or add a noun after this (this delay, this mistake).

test.q: Which revision makes “The clinic cut its hours and raised its fees, and this angered patients” clear?
options: The clinic cut its hours and raised its fees, and this really angered patients.
The clinic cut its hours and raised its fees, which angered patients.
The fee increase angered patients after the clinic cut its hours.
The clinic cut its hours and raised its fees; this angered patients.
test.why: Naming “the fee increase” tells the reader exactly which change angered patients.

whyNot.0: Adding “really” leaves “this” pointing to either change or both.
whyNot.1: Swapping “this” for “which” keeps the same broad reference.
whyNot.3: A semicolon changes the punctuation but not the unclear “this.”

explain.body: Once a sentence refers to people in one person (I, you, one, a student, they), keep it. “One ... you” and “a student ... you” are shifts.

rows.label: Example
values: If a nurse rests, you heal.

test.q: Which sentence keeps the pronoun person consistent?
options: When students arrive late, you lose the chance to test.
When one arrives late, you lose the chance to test.
When students arrive late, they lose the chance to test.
When a student arrives late, we lose the chance to test.
test.why: “Students” and “they” are both third person plural.

whyNot.0: Shifts from third person (students) to second person (you).
whyNot.1: Shifts from third person (one) to second person (you).
whyNot.3: Shifts from third person (a student) to first person (we).
